blocks.text: 1.1 Mandate and objective

Wesgro commissioned research and an action plan to "double international tourist arrivals to the Western Cape by 2035" (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p4). The evidence reframes that goal as growth to 2.5 million arrivals, paced by gateway capacity in the summer peak and by demand in the green season.
Wesgro acts through partners to create jobs

Wesgro promotes tourism, trade and investment for Cape Town and the Western Cape, so the tourism goal sits inside a wider economic brief. Its mission is to work "together with partners, drive inclusive and sustainable economic growth, strengthen competitiveness, and create jobs in Cape Town and the Western Cape". Its vision is to "be a leading regional tourism, trade and investment promotion agency" (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p5). Two points in the mission shape the recommendations: growth is a means to jobs, and Wesgro acts through partners rather than holding the levers itself.

Four of Wesgro's eight strategy statements bear directly on this study (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p5). The first sets the destination proposition: Cape Town and the Western Cape "top of mind as a leading business and tourism destination with premium products and services". The fourth names new markets and buyers in China, ASEAN, India, Brazil and the Middle East, "while maintaining a continued focus on established markets". The sixth commits Wesgro to "Track and address systemic challenges influencing economic competitiveness", and the seventh to "Provide economic data, insights & analytics for the Western Cape". The growth-market work in focus area 4 centres on two of them: India and China, whose travellers already reach Cape Town through Gulf and African hubs (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p46, p48). The growth model's acceleration group holds the Gulf, China, India and Brazil (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p20).
Of four ambitions, only arrivals has a target the evidence supports

The objective, set in November 2025, is "To develop an evidence-based tourism strategy that will double international tourist arrivals to the Western Cape by 2035". It continues: "through a holistic approach that drives demand, strengthens supply and enables inclusive, sustainable and geographically dispersed growth aligned with WESGRO's strategic priorities" (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p4). The research builds the evidence the objective calls for, and Chapters 3 and 4 turn it into recommendations and initiatives. The objective fixes the three pillars the report keeps throughout: demand, supply and enablement. Of its terms, only the doubling did not survive the evidence.

Four headline ambitions sat under the objective: 2.8 million international visitors, 300,000 tourism-linked jobs, 10,000 SMMEs onboarded and twice the airlift and cruise volumes (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p4). The report carries all four forward. The evidence reframed the first and changed how the other three are measured.

**Arrivals.** The growth model tested the doubling and supports 2.2 million to 2.5 million by 2035. From 1,498,829 arrivals in 2025, its base case reaches 2,175,778 by 2035 and its accelerated case 2,516,282, above a conservative floor of 1,822,634 (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p20; this source prints the same 2035 points from a 2024 base). The base case holds Wesgro's effort at 2025 intensity, with selective frequency gains and continued hub expansion. The accelerated case needs confirmed direct routes to India and China, above-baseline activation and more hub capacity into Cape Town; without the routes, volume reverts to base (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p18, p19). Growth to 2.5 million is that case rounded, and it is the goal the report carries.

Even the base case outruns the model's air access. The model draws a seat line at 1.8 million inbound seats, and the base case first passes it at the 2030 year point, at 1,802,929 arrivals (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p20). The line is an assumption rather than a measured cap. In practice the runway binds first, at peak hours (section 1.3). Growth to 2.5 million is therefore a supply programme before it is a marketing programme.

**Jobs.** The ambition was 300,000 tourism-linked jobs, yet the evidence holds no Western Cape tourism employment figure (section 2.4). Jobs therefore enter Chapter 5 without a baseline. Wesgro and DEDAT should commission a labour analysis in 2027 to set one (focus area 20).

**SMMEs.** The ambition was 10,000 SMMEs onboarded, with no baseline or definition printed [Wesgro to confirm the baseline count and definition of SMMEs onboarded]. The action plan treats it as community inclusion, measured in visitor spend reaching priority communities rather than a count of firms (section 2.4 and Chapter 5).

**Airlift and cruise.** The ambition was twice the airlift and cruise volumes. Section 3.2.1 sets airlift as the seats and routes needed to lift the model's 1.8 million seat line (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p20). It sets cruise as calls and ports. Wesgro's plan targets 250 ship calls over FY26 to FY30, or 50 a year (Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p20). [Summary of Findings, 14 Oct 2026: Cruise Cape Town to confirm that the deck's 250 calls are the plan's five-year total.] The cruise baseline is 79 vessels in the 2024/25 season (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p37). Of the four ambitions, only arrivals has a target the evidence supports today. The other three go forward with their baselines still to be fixed.
Wesgro's five-year targets and the growth case

Wesgro's FY26 to FY30 plan sets six tourism targets, each over the plan's five years (Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p20). Two of them also measure Wesgro's strategic outcomes for leisure tourism and business events: 800,000 to 1 million new international tourist arrivals and 161 business event bids secured, worth an estimated R4.5 billion (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p6). The other four are 250 ship calls, 10 new air routes, three international tourism marketing campaigns and 12,500 international tourism trade engagements. A new route is a scheduled international service flying to and from Cape Town for the first time (Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p59). The table sets each target beside what this report carries.

blocks.text: The five-year period decides how the arrivals target compares with the growth case, and the plan can be read two ways. By 2030 the base case adds about 304,000 yearly arrivals to the 2025 level and the accelerated case about 443,000 (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19, p20; computed). Read as a rise in yearly arrivals, Wesgro's 800,000 to 1 million is 2.6 to 3.3 times the base case's gain and about twice the accelerated case's (computed). On that reading no modelled path delivers it by 2030. Read as extra arrivals summed over the five years, as the plan counts its other targets, the base case adds about 890,000 and meets it (computed). On the first reading Wesgro's target sharpens the case that growth is a supply programme; on the second it matches the base path. [Wesgro to confirm whether the arrivals target is a rise in yearly arrivals by 2030 or a sum over the five years, and the base year from which new arrivals are counted.]

The activity targets, by contrast, hold or fall below today's pace. Each year they ask for about 32 bids, 50 ship calls and two new routes. The recent pace is 36 bids secured and 79 vessels in 2024/25, and about three route launches a year since 2015 on Cape Town Air Access's count (Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p20; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p36; Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p37; Cape Town Air Access, Letsema Update, Nov 2025, slide 5; computed). The cruise target sits below the last season partly because its base appears to leave out the ships rerouted in 2023/24. The plan rounds up an annual average of 47 calls and notes that 20 of the 67 calls in 2023/24 were ships rerouted by the Middle East conflict (Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p20). The 47 equals 67 less 20 (computed). [Wesgro to confirm how the 47-call average was set.] Trade engagements stay at 2,500 a year, flat on FY24. Any step change sits in the outcome, not in the activity.

Wesgro calls the outcome behind its arrivals target "growth in leisure tourism consideration in international and local markets" (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p6; Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p19). Yet consideration is not the constraint: about 97 million high-value travellers are interested in South Africa, and about 1.4 million convert (section 1.3). When it next revises its plan, Wesgro should state the outcome as conversion and value.

The business-events metric ties to the action plan's green-season focus (focus area 2). International association meetings in Cape Town rose from 33 in 2022 to 58 in 2024 and are "primarily hosted between May and November" (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p26). That window overlaps the green season, April to September (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p25), but 74 of the 136 meetings from 2022 to 2024 fell between September and November (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p37, computed). Bids must therefore pull meetings into the trough months (section 3.1). Chapter 5 tracks the nearest indicators: international arrivals and association meetings in Cape Town (T1-01 and T2-02).
Alignment rests on value and spread as well as arrivals

The study's contract requires this report and its recommendations to align with two documents: the Growth for Jobs Strategy (G4J) and Wesgro's FY26 to FY30 plan (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p22; the requirement itself sits in SLA Annexure B, clause 1.1.14.2). This report is the Final Research Report under clause 1.1.14, and Chapter 5 answers the monitoring and evaluation clauses 1.1.4 and 1.1.10 [clause references to be checked against the signed SLA Annexure B, whose wording is not in hand].

The Growth for Jobs Strategy 2023, approved by Cabinet, designates tourism a primary tradable sector for the province (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p34; Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p5). Wesgro states the G4J arrivals target two ways. To the parliamentary committee it gave 3 million international tourist arrivals by 2035 on the South African Tourism basis (Wesgro, presentation to the parliamentary committee, 1 Apr 2026; public source). Its FY26 to FY30 plan gives 3 million by 2030, as the 2 million of 2019 plus 1 million (Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p20). [G4J 2023 document to be read and the 3 million target confirmed against it.] On South African Tourism's count the province received 1,538,142 in 2025 (Wesgro Research, Western Cape Tourism Performance: Annual 2025, from SA Tourism data; public source; the 2025 count rose 11.1% on the year), still below the 2 million of 2019 on which G4J builds. On either date the 3 million sits above both of the model's paths. Part of the gap is method: G4J adds 1 million to the 2019 count, while the model builds up market by market against the seats the gateway can carry. Part may be measure, because what the model counts is not yet confirmed (see the closing note). Until it is, the 2.5 million cannot be set directly against the 3 million.

Growth for Jobs also sets a value test. It calls tourism the province's most obvious service export and aims to triple the value of the province's exports of goods and services, tourism included, by 2035 (Growth for Jobs Strategy 2023, p11, p14). On the model's base case, direct foreign spend rises about 1.5 times from the modelled R27.12bn of 2024 to R40.6bn in 2035, in constant 2024 rand (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p24; computed). G4J's tripling covers all exports from its own base year, and the model's 1.5 times is tourism spend in constant 2024 rand, so the two cannot yet be compared. Alignment will still be tested on value as well as arrivals, so Chapter 5 tracks spend, season and spread beside arrivals.

Wesgro's FY26 to FY30 plan is the second test, and its six targets let alignment rest on numbers rather than principle. The timing fits too. Chapter 4 sets its first decision gate at the end of 2028, inside Wesgro's plan period and before the base case crosses the model's seat line. That gate is the point to map the initiatives' outputs to the plan's six targets and to state which of them the action plan would raise.

The Tourism Blueprint 2030, the province's sector roadmap, is not one of the contract's two tests, but it points the same way. Its objectives map onto the action plan's three pillars: numbers, yield and profile in demand; infrastructure, spread, district development and customer experience in supply; partnerships and ease of business in enablement (Tourism Blueprint 2030, p9). Only its renewed focus on domestic markets lies outside this study's international mandate.
How the report counts arrivals

Four kinds of arrivals figure circulate around this study: ambitions, airport passengers, South African Tourism's tourist arrivals and the model's arrivals. Appendix A2 lists every such figure with its base. The report keeps them apart under three rules. Airport passenger arrivals at Cape Town International, by fiscal year, are the baseline and tracking series, with FY24/25 at 1.44 million (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p26, p41; the source uses Cape Town air arrivals as its provincial proxy). The model's 2025 base of 1,498,829 and its 2035 points are the target series. The model also splits markets differently from South African Tourism. Over 2022 to 2024 South African Tourism's yearly averages for India and China were a quarter to a fifth of the model's 2025 values, and France's about three times, though the periods differ (Wesgro Research, Tourism Source Market Analysis, Nov 2025, p4; Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p21, p22; computed). [Open item: Skift to confirm in writing what the model counts (SA Tourism tourist arrivals, ACSA passengers including returning residents or OAG origin-and-destination flows) and how the Hubs group is built.] South African Tourism's provincial count is used to read across to the G4J target and, through Wesgro Research's source market analysis, to measure the province's share of global and market travel from 2022 to 2024. The report quotes the series side by side and never adds one to the other [model owner to confirm the series and year basis behind the 2025 base of 1,498,829].
